title: Count Connected Components in LCM Graph
statement: Build an undirected graph with one node per entry of `nums` (the values are all different). Nodes `i` and `j` are joined by an edge exactly when the least common multiple of `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` is at most `threshold`. Return how many connected components the graph has, that is, how many maximal groups of nodes are linked to each other by paths. A node without edges is a component by itself.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every pair of numbers builds up to n² edges, far too many for 10^5 values. Look at a single edge instead: if `lcm(a, b) <= threshold`, then that lcm is a common multiple of `a` and `b` no larger than `threshold`. Conversely, any common multiple `m <= threshold` is itself a multiple of the lcm, so the lcm is at most `m`. So two numbers are adjacent exactly when they share a multiple at or below `threshold`. Joining every number to each of its multiples in a union-find over the values `1..threshold` therefore merges exactly the numbers that are connected. A number above `threshold` has an lcm with anything at least itself, so it stays alone.

## Approach

1. Make `parent` a union-find over `0..threshold`, every value its own root.
2. For each `num`: if it exceeds `threshold`, count it in `isolated`. Otherwise call `union(num, multiple)` for `multiple = 2·num, 3·num, ...` up to `threshold`.
3. Put `find(num)` of every `num <= threshold` into the set `roots`.
4. Return `isolated + roots.size`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 4, 8, 3, 9]`, `threshold = 5`.

- `2`: its only multiple up to 5 is `4`, so `union(2, 4)`.
- `4` and `3`: their first multiples, 8 and 6, are past 5.
- `8` and `9` exceed 5, so `isolated = 2`.

The roots of 2, 4 and 3 are `{4, 3}`, so the answer is `2 + 2 = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + T log T) union-find operations with T = `threshold`: a value `v` visits T / v multiples, and summing T / v over the values gives at most T times a harmonic number. Path halving keeps each `find` short (amortized O(log T) at worst).
- Space: O(T) for `parent`.

## Pitfalls

- Values above `threshold` do not fit in `parent`; count them before indexing.
- Multiples that are not in `nums` act as bridges but are not nodes: count roots of `nums` only.
- If you do compute an lcm (say, to test one pair), divide first, `a / gcd(a, b) * b`, in 64-bit integers: the product of two values near 10^9 overflows a 32-bit int. The union-find approach never needs one.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parent` | union-find parent of each value `0..threshold` |
| `find`, `union` | root lookup with path halving, and merging two sets |
| `isolated` | numbers above `threshold`, each its own component |
| `multiple` | a multiple of `num` up to `threshold` |
| `roots` | distinct roots of the numbers at or below `threshold` |

narration.2: Every value from 0 to threshold starts as its own set; larger values never get an entry.
narration.4: Climb until reaching a value that is its own parent, the root.
narration.5: Path halving: point x at its grandparent so later lookups are shorter.
narration.8: x is now the root of its set.
narration.13: Merge the two sets if they are different.
narration.17: Go through the numbers once to link each to its multiples.
narration.18: A number above threshold has an lcm of at least itself with anything...
narration.19: ...so it is a component on its own.
narration.22: Visit every multiple of num up to threshold; two numbers dividing the same multiple have an lcm no larger than it.
narration.23: Link num with this multiple, which bridges it to every other number dividing the multiple.
narration.28: Look at every number again to see which set it ended up in.
narration.29: Numbers in the same component share a root, so collecting roots counts components.
narration.31: Lone numbers above the threshold plus the distinct roots of the rest.
